sense: put to use (a rule, a remedy)

terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation; with ad or in and the accusative, or the dative
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.134: sī sēriīs, sevēritātem adhibeat, sī jocōsīs, lepōrem
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to put a thing to a determinate use, to apply, to use or employ”, with intention, unlike ūtī. That a rule applies to someone is ad aliquem pertinet (see concern).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with ad and the accusative, or the dative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.7 (Lewis & Short): meum cōnsilium accommodābō ad tuum
Cic. Amic. 81: ad quās sē applicent
terms.comment: Classically to put one thing against another, or with sē to attach oneself to someone; not to apply a rule.

phrases.latin: sī sēriīs, sevēritātem adhibeat, sī jocōsīs, lepōrem
phrases.english: To serious things let him bring gravity, to playful things charm.

phrases.latin: habenda ratiō valētūdinis, ūtendum exercitātiōnibus modicīs, tantum cibī et pōtiōnis adhibendum ut reficiantur vīrēs, nōn opprimantur
phrases.english: We must look after our health, take moderate exercise, and take just enough food and drink to restore our strength, not to crush it.

phrases.latin: quod etiam rūsticīs nōtum est, quī frondibus tenerīs nōn putant adhibendam esse falcem
phrases.english: Even countrymen know this: they do not think the pruning-knife should be put to tender shoots.

sources: Lewis & Short: adhibeo · Lewis & Short: accommodo · Lewis & Short: applico
